nodes.text: The Government of India asserted an ownership basis originating from acquisition under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904. It maintained that the suit properties were recorded in its name and that the Wakf Board could not validly assert ownership over them.

limitations: TRUE establishes that the Government advanced this original-title claim, not that the asserted acquisition was independently proved by the pleading.
The pleading does not provide a verified acquisition date or a separately documented acquisition transaction for each property.
The Government's claimed ownership is distinct from its alternative adverse-possession theory.

nodes.text: The Government of India alternatively sought recognition of ownership on the ground that it had perfected title by adverse possession. This was presented as an alternative basis in the original suits alongside its original-title position.

limitations: TRUE records the assertion of an alternative legal basis, not successful proof of adverse possession.
The reported pleading does not identify a verified starting date of hostile possession.
The assertion does not itself establish recognition or renunciation of another ownership basis.

nodes.text: The Wakf Board and other defendants advanced a historical ownership account involving Peer Mahabari Khandayat, construction of a mosque, long-standing treatment of property as Wakf, and management by religious successors. They relied on that account in opposition to the Government's ownership claim.

metadata.time_scope: Claimed historical origin around AD 1304 or the thirteenth century and claimed continuity for approximately seven centuries.
limitations: TRUE establishes the existence and content of the opposing historical claim only.
The historical account was not independently authenticated by the supplied material.
The claim concerning mosque construction and religious succession cannot automatically be extended as individually proved historical facts to all three distinct properties.
The Supreme Court separately evaluated whether concrete evidence supported the competing ownership claim.

nodes.text: The opposing defendants claimed to possess appropriate sanads establishing Wakf character and asserted that the relevant property had been entered in the Wakf Register.

limitations: The existence of an assertion about sanads does not establish that authenticated sanads were produced.
The independent contents, dates and legal effects of the alleged sanads are not provided.
The reported Wakf Register assertion does not itself resolve the disputed ownership.

nodes.text: The Wakf Board asserted ownership through its April 1976 notification, the July 1976 Gazette publication, and a subsequent revenue enquiry concluding that the property was Wakf property. It also contested the Government's acquisition account.

metadata.time_scope: Notifications dated 21 April 1976 and 8 July 1976; subsequent enquiry date not established.
limitations: TRUE records the Board's asserted legal effect of the notifications and enquiry.
The April notification and July Gazette publication are distinct reported instruments.
The precise evidentiary contents of the underlying instruments and enquiry record were not independently supplied.
The asserted legal effect was not accepted merely because the instruments were alleged to exist.

nodes.text: The Trial Court found, on oral and documentary evidence, that the Government had taken the properties as ancient monuments before the local Survey Department's introduction, had acquired them as long ago as approximately 1900, and had continued preserving, possessing, enjoying and managing them.

metadata.time_scope: Acquisition described by the Trial Court as occurring as long ago as 1900; continuing possession and management thereafter.
limitations: This is the Trial Court's reported finding, not a separately authenticated acquisition transaction.
The approximate 1900 date is preserved as stated and is not silently reconciled with the Government's reliance on the 1904 Act.
Acquisition, preservation, management and possession retain distinct legal meanings.
The judgment does not identify separate acquisition instruments for each of the three properties.

nodes.text: The Trial Court found that the Wakf Board had declared the properties Wakf properties without properly following the applicable Wakf Act provisions and prescribed procedure. The Trial Court also considered the defendants' evidence insufficient to establish their asserted continuing possession.

limitations: This is a lower-court finding, not an independent review of the Wakf statutory procedure.
The finding about insufficient proof of continued possession does not establish that no historical possession ever occurred.
A procedural defect in a Wakf declaration is distinct from affirmative proof of the Government's original title.

nodes.text: The High Court Division Bench reviewed the matter and affirmed the Trial Court's findings concerning the disputed properties.

limitations: This records the appellate affirmance and does not transform the Trial Court's findings into independently inspected source evidence.
The High Court's separate acceptance of an adverse-possession ground is recorded independently.

nodes.text: The High Court treated adverse possession as an additional basis supporting relief for the Government. That determination was subsequently questioned by the Supreme Court.

limitations: TRUE denotes that the High Court accepted this alternative ground, not that adverse possession was ultimately established.
This finding must not be attributed to the Supreme Court.
The original High Court judgment was not separately supplied.

nodes.text: The Wakf Board sought an opportunity to produce further important documents. The High Court rejected the request, and the Supreme Court found no justification for interference, referring to earlier opportunities and the failure to identify documents whose production would materially affect the matter.

metadata.time_scope: Request raised at the High Court appellate stage and reiterated before the Supreme Court.
limitations: The request to introduce additional evidence does not authenticate the allegedly available documents.
The missing documents' exact contents and probative effects remain unknown.
The rejection does not prove that every underlying historical assertion was false.
The finding is relevant to the evidentiary record available for the ownership dispute.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court found no concrete evidence on record supporting the appellants' ownership claim and declined to accept historical assertions about the religious figure, mosque construction and descendants' possession without substantiating evidence and records.

limitations: The finding concerns the insufficiency of the opposing ownership evidence in the judicial record.
It does not establish the historical nonexistence of Peer Mahabari Khandayat, mosque construction or religious management.
It does not independently establish the Government's title without the affirmative documentary and testimonial evidence.

nodes.text: The judgment reports that Exhibit P1, a relevant copy of the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments, identifies the suit property and refers to the Government as its owner.

limitations: TRUE establishes the contents of the register as reported in the judgment.
The underlying exhibit was not separately supplied or authenticated.
The entry is not independently treated as an instrument that conclusively creates title.
The judgment does not reproduce parcel-by-parcel register entries or registration dates.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court expressly recorded that the manner of the Government's acquisition was not under challenge when assessing the evidentiary significance of the protected-monuments register.

limitations: This is the court's express characterization of the challenge to the manner of acquisition.
The appellants nevertheless disputed the Government's ownership and described its acquisition account as concocted.
The finding does not identify the precise acquisition instrument, date or statutory steps.
A limited absence of challenge to the acquisition manner must not be converted into an admission of every disputed ownership proposition.

nodes.text: Given the unchallenged manner of acquisition as recorded by the Supreme Court, the court treated the protected-monuments register entry as valid evidentiary support for the Government's asserted acquisition under the relevant provisions of the Ancient Monuments Act.

limitations: The evidentiary inference is expressly contextual.
This premise does not independently establish an acquisition transaction or complete statutory compliance.
The register's evidentiary value must remain distinct from the ultimate assessment of title.
The court also referred to assumption of guardianship as another possible means of gaining possession.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court explained that gaining possession could occur either through acquisition or through assumption of guardianship under section 4 of the Ancient Monuments Act. The supplied judgment does not separately establish which precise statutory transaction occurred for every property.

limitations: TRUE applies to the court's statement that these are possible alternative possession bases.
It does not establish that both mechanisms occurred.
Assumption of guardianship must not be treated as identical to acquisition of ownership.
Neither a particular guardianship event nor its date is independently established.
The precise statutory mechanism and its property-specific application remain unresolved.

nodes.text: The judgment reports that Exhibit P2, the relevant city survey record extracts, supports the Government's case and shows the property standing in the Government's name.

limitations: The underlying city survey extracts were not separately supplied.
The record's complete contents and dates are unknown.
A city survey entry is reported evidentiary support and is not automatically equivalent to a conclusive title instrument.
The judgment does not provide separate reconstructed entries for the three properties.

nodes.text: Syed Abdul Nabi, identified as power-of-attorney holder for original defendants 2A and 2B, testified that the Government was in possession of the disputed property.

limitations: TRUE means the witness reportedly gave this testimony.
The complete witness deposition and cross-examination were not supplied.
Possession testimony is not independently authenticated proof of every asserted duration or ownership consequence.
The judgment does not allocate this testimony separately to each parcel.

nodes.text: Syed Abdul Nabi also testified that the property had been declared a protected monument, that a signboard indicated this status, and that the Government had constructed the present building at its expense.

limitations: The proposition records reported testimony rather than independently verified construction expenditure.
The exact construction date, building identification and funding records are not supplied.
Protected-monument status and government construction do not independently establish acquisition of title.
This is additional evidence considered alongside the ownership documents and possession testimony.

nodes.text: Following its combined assessment of Exhibit P1, Exhibit P2 and Syed Abdul Nabi's deposition, the Supreme Court concluded that the Government had absolute ownership and continuous possession for approximately a century and that its title was valid. It characterized the disputed property as Government property rather than Wakf property.

metadata.time_scope: Continuous possession assessed by the Supreme Court as lasting approximately one century up to the judgment; precise beginning date not independently established.
limitations: This is the Supreme Court's affirmative evaluation of title and possession, not a final-disposition premise.
The conclusion was reached through a combined evidentiary assessment and must not be represented as an automatic consequence of any single document.
The court's approximately one-century possession finding is not itself proof of all requirements of adverse possession.
The supporting exhibits and deposition are known through the judgment's descriptions, not independent authentication.
The finding should remain separate from the High Court's additional adverse-possession reasoning.
The precise acquisition mechanism, acquisition date and individual parcel transactions are not established by the supplied excerpts.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court stated that adverse possession requires hostile possession asserting title against the true owner, together with actual, visible, exclusive, open and continuous possession of legally sufficient duration. Exclusive physical possession and animus possidendi were identified as particularly important.

limitations: This is a legal standard, not a factual finding that hostile possession occurred in the present suits.
The requirements involve contextual factual and legal evaluation.
Long possession and ordinary ownership-related possession are not automatically hostile possession.
The judgment does not establish an applicable statutory commencement date for adverse possession in these suits.
The rule cannot be reduced to a deterministic checklist.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court placed on the party invoking adverse possession the obligation to plead and establish all necessary facts. It identified the date possession began, its character, the other party's knowledge, its duration and whether it was open and undisturbed as relevant matters.

limitations: This is the express burden relating to a party asserting adverse possession.
No complete general burden framework for the competing acquisition-based title claim is inferred.
A failure to plead or prove a fact is not evidence that the alleged event was physically impossible or never occurred.
The requirements must be assessed contextually rather than through automatic Boolean conjunction.

nodes.text: The Government asserted both an original-title basis and an alternative adverse-possession basis concerning the same suit properties. The Supreme Court discussed the inconsistency of such theories and the principle that adverse possession does not begin to operate until the earlier title basis is renounced.

limitations: TRUE establishes the existence of the two alternative theories and the legal tension they raise.
The quoted inconsistency and renunciation principle is reported through the Supreme Court's discussion of precedent.
The actual occurrence, legal effectiveness and timing of any renunciation are not separately established.
Renunciation must not be presumed absent solely because the alternative theories were advanced.
The reported contractual circumstances of Mohan Lal are not facts of the present suits.
The tension alone is not an independently sufficient finding that adverse possession failed.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court expressly found that the Government had not specifically pleaded and proved possession excluding the Wakf Board with the intention to possess as owner. The finding concerns the inadequacy of pleading and proof of hostile exclusion and animus.

limitations: TRUE means that the Supreme Court identified the specified pleading-and-proof deficiency.
It does not mean that Government possession was disproved.
It does not establish the factual impossibility of exclusive or hostile possession.
The finding must remain distinct from the Government's ordinary possession supported by documentary and testimonial evidence.
The original pleadings were not independently supplied.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court identified a further deficiency concerning the Government's failure specifically to plead and prove the Wakf Board's alleged earlier title as part of the adverse-possession theory.

limitations: The court's finding concerns the absence of specific pleading and proof of earlier opposing title.
It does not independently establish that the Wakf Board actually held such earlier title.
The opposing ownership claim was separately found to lack concrete evidentiary support.
The court's reference to earlier title must not be converted into an admission of the Board's ownership.
This is a separate material deficiency within the same adverse-possession analysis.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court found that the relevant point in time of the supposed dispossession had not been specifically pleaded and proved as part of the Government's alternative adverse-possession case.

limitations: TRUE establishes the court's finding of missing specific pleading and proof about the temporal aspect.
No dispossession date can be recovered from the supplied material.
The absence of a pleaded or proved date does not itself establish that no dispossession occurred.
The approximately one-century period of Government possession cannot be substituted for a proven commencement date of hostile possession.
The judgment's wording is preserved without inventing a separately authenticated dispossession event.

nodes.text: After identifying the missing specific pleading and proof concerning exclusive hostile possession, the Wakf Board's alleged earlier title and the timing of dispossession, the Supreme Court concluded that the Government's alternative adverse-possession plea was unsustainable.

limitations: This records the Supreme Court's ground-specific conclusion, not the final appellate disposition.
The decision rests on the judicially identified deficiencies and contextual adverse-possession requirements.
It does not imply that the Government never possessed the property.
It does not independently determine every possible adverse-possession element or a specific statutory limitation period.
The record does not separately establish whether legally effective renunciation occurred.
The failure of this alternative ground is distinct from the affirmative original-title evaluation.

nodes.text: The Supreme Court specifically criticized the High Court's reliance on adverse possession while retaining its separately expressed affirmative assessment of Government title based on Exhibit P1, Exhibit P2 and the reported testimony. The criticism was limited to the adverse-possession ground.

limitations: The phrase this ground refers to the alternative adverse-possession ground.
The proposition is limited to the distinction between the two title theories.
It does not assert that the failed adverse-possession plea affirmatively proves original title.
The original-title finding must remain grounded in its own documentary and testimonial support.
This premise does not rely on the Supreme Court's final dismissal of the appeals.
No independent determination of every appellate-relief requirement is attempted.

CTS No.36, Ward No.VI, Macca Masjid, Bijapur
CTS No.35, Ward No.VI, Water Tower, Bijapur
Exhibit P1, relevant copy of the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments maintained by the Executive Engineer
Exhibit P2, relevant extracts of city survey or CTS records
Syed Abdul Nabi, power-of-attorney holder for defendants 2A and 2B in the original suit
Peer Mahabari Khandayat, Arabian religious figure invoked in the opposing parties' historical ownership account

CASE NO.:
Appeal (civil)  16899 of 1996
PETITIONER:
Karnataka Board of Wakf
RESPONDENT:
Government of India & Ors.
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 16/04/2004
BENCH:
S. RAJENDRA BABU & G.P. MATHUR
JUDGMENT:
J U D G M E N T [With C.A.Nos. 16900/1996 & 16895/1996] RAJENDRA BABU, J. :

> Three suits were filed by the first respondent in each of these cases seeking for a declaration that notifications issued by the Karnataka Board of Wakf, i.e., the appellant before us, showing some of the defendants to be illegal and void or in the alternative, to declare the first respondent as owner of the suit properties on the ground that they have perfected their title by adverse possession and consequential relief for permanent injunction.

There are three sets of properties in each of these three matters. One is CTS No.24 of Ward No.VI, described as "Karimuddin's Mosque", another is CTS No.36 of Ward No.VI, described as "Macca Masjid" and the other is CTS No.35 of Ward No. VI, described as " Water Tower". All of them were situated at Bijapur.

> The claim made by the first respondent is that they acquired the suit property under the cite10†Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 cite10†(Ancient Monuments Act ) and a notification has been published in that regard and the suit property had been entered in the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments incharge of the Executive Engineer.

Thereafter, the Government of India enacted the cite11†Ancient Monuments And Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and the suit property came to be under the management of the Department of Archeological Survey, Government of India.

It is asserted by the first respondent that in all the relevant records, the name of the Government of India has been shown as the owner of the suit property and that they came to know that the defendants got published a notification No.KTW/531/ASR-74/7490 dated 21.4.1976 showing that the suit property as having been declared as 'Wakf Property' in terms of cite12†section 26 of the Wakf Act, 1954 and was also stated to have been published in the Gazette.

Inasmuch as the suit property since inception was under the ownership of the plaintiff with lawful possession thereof, defendants could not have made any claim thereto nor get the same declared as Wakf property.

The defendants contested this claim of the plaintiffs in the original suits and that after following due procedure publication has been made in the Karnataka Gazette in terms of cite13†Section 67 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act and the order passed by the concerned officer is binding on the plaintiff and, therefore, the plaintiff cannot claim any ownership on the ground of adverse possession.

While this is the stand of the Wakf Board, the appellant before us, and the other defendants described as to be "mutawallis" of the Wakf property, stated that one of the Arab Preachers, Peer Mahabari Khandayat came as a Missionary to Deccan as early as AD 1304 and occupied whole Arkilla and erected "Mecca Masjid" according to established customs to offer prayer which is surrounded by a vast open area.

The said property had all along for seven centuries been treated as Wakfs and have been since after the time of Peer, managed, looked after and maintained by Sajjada Nashin from time to time. No one has interfered with their right.

They claim that they have appropriate sanads to show that the property in question is Wakf property and that another portion of the suit property also belongs to the Darga of Peer Mahabari Khandayat and Chinni Mahabari Khandayat Darga Arbkilla, Bijapur and, therefore, the same has been appropriately entered in the Wakf Register.

The trial court raised several issues in the matter and gave a finding that on a consideration of the oral and documentary evidence in the case it is clear that even prior to the introduction of the Survey Department at Bijapur, the Government of India had taken these properties as ancient monuments and they are protecting them by keeping appropriate watch over these monuments but now the defendants have come forward contending that these properties are Wakf properties and they have nothing to show that even after the demise of Peer Mahabari Khandyat they remained in the possession of the same.

The properties in question were acquired by the Government of India as long back as 1900 and they started preserving them as important historical monuments and they remained in possession and enjoyment of them. This was clear both from oral and documentary evidence and on that basis, the Trial Court held that they are owning and managing the suit properties.

The Trial Court also gave a finding that the Wakf Board itself declared these properties as Wakf properties without properly following the relevant provisions of the cite14†Wakf Act and without following due procedure prescribed therein and in a case where there is a dispute as to who is a stranger to the Wakf, a mere declaration by the Wakf Board will not bind such person and on that basis the Trial Court decreed the suit.

The matter was carried in appeal. A Division Bench of the High Court examined the matter once over again and affirmed the findings of the Trial Court. The Division Bench also noticed that at the end of the arguments the appellant made a submission that as they have not produced some of the important documents, the matter may be remanded to the Trial Court in order to enable them to produce the said documents and with a direction to the Trial Court for a fresh disposal in accordance with law.

The High Court did not allow the plea raised by the appellant that there are documents in question which will go to the root of the matter or which would be necessary in terms of Order XLI, Rule 27, cite15†CPC to permit them to adduce further evidence and on that basis rejected that claim. The High Court affirmed the various findings given by the Trial Court.

In the circumstances, the learned counsel for the appellant, reiterated the claim made before the High Court that they should be permitted to adduce further evidence before the court to substantiate their claim but when the matters were pending before the Trial Court and the High Court they had ample opportunity to do so.

If they had to produce appropriate documents, they could have done so and also it is not clear as to the nature of the documents which they seek to produce which will tilt the matter one way or the other.

The scope of Order XLI, Rule 27, cite15†CPC is very clear to the effect that the parties to an appeal shall not be entitled to produce additional evidence, whether oral or documentary, unless they have shown that in spite of due diligence, they could not produce such documents and such documents are required to enable the court to pronounce proper judgment. In this view of the matter, we do not think there is any justification for us to interfere with the orders of the High Court.

However, in view of the arguments addressed by the learned counsel for the appellant, we have also gone into various aspects of the matter and have given another look at the matter and our findings are that the view taken by the High Court is justified. However, one aspect needs to be noticed. The High Court need not have stated that the first respondent is entitled to the relief even on the basis of adverse possession. We propose to examine this aspect.

The case advanced by the Appellants is; that one Arabian saint Mahabari Khandayat came to Bijapur by around 13th century, acquired certain properties (suit property) and constructed 'Mecca Mosque' which is under the management of the lineal descendants of the said saint; that by virtue of Notification bearing No. KTW/531 ASR/74/7490 dated 21/04/1976 issued by Appellant and Karnataka Gazette Notification page No.

608/Part VI dated 08/07/1976 they became absolute owners and title holders of the suit property; that pursuant to the circulars dated 08/06/1978 and 22/01/1979 the Deputy Commissioner of the Districts were instructed to handover possession of any Wakf Properties that are under the possession of any Government Department; that by virtue of the said circular Assistant Commissioner, Bijapur held enquiry under cite13†section 67 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 and arrived at the conclusion that the suit property is a Wakf Property; that the alleged acquisition by the Respondent itself is a concocted story; that the Notification and the Gazette publication itself is a notice to all concerned and the Respondent failed to reply to this notice; that the original suit is bad by limitation; that the original suit itself is not maintainable since there is no notice under section 56 of the Old Wakf Act; that the plea regarding title of the suit property by the Respondent and the plea of adverse possession is mutually exclusive; that therefore the appeal is to be allowed.

Pertaining to the ownership claim of Appellants over the suit property there is no concrete evidence on record. The contention of Appellants that one Arabian saint Mahabari Khandayat came to India and built the Mosque and his lineal descendents possessed the property cannot be accepted if it is not substantiated by evidence and records. As far as a title suit of civil nature is concerned there is no room for historical facts and claims.

Reliance on borderline historical facts will lead to erroneous conclusions. The question for resolution herein is the factum of ownership, possession and title over the suit property. Only admissible evidence and records could be of assistance to prove this.

On the other hand, Respondent produced the relevant copy of the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments maintained by the Executive Engineer in charge of the Ancient Monuments (Exb P1) wherein the suit property is mentioned and the Government is referred to as the owner.

Since the manner of acquisition is not under challenge the entry in the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments could be treated as a valid proof for their case regarding the acquisition of suit property under the appropriate provisions of the cite10†Ancient Monuments Act . Gaining of possession could be either by acquisition or by assuming guardianship as provided under cite16†section 4 thereof. Relevant extracts of Exb P2 - CTS records fortifies their case.

It shows that the property stands in the name of Respondent. Moreover, the evidence of Syed Abdul Nabi who is the power of attorney holder (of defendants 2A and 2B in the Original suit) shows that the suit property has been declared as a protected monument and there is a signboard to this effect in the suit property. He also deposed that the Government is in possession of the suit property and the Government at its expenditure constructed present building in the suit property.

On a conjoint analysis of Exb P1, P2 and deposition of Syed Abdul Nabi, it could be safely concluded that the Respondent is in absolute ownership and continuous possession of the suit property for the last about one century. Their title is valid. The suit property is government property and not of a Wakf character.

The Old Wakf Act is enacted "for the better administration and supervision of wakfs." Under section 4 of the Old Wakf Act, Survey Commissioner(s) could only make a "survey of wakf properties existing in the State at the date of commencement of this Act." Wakf Board could exercise its rights only over existing wakf properties. Since the suit property itself is not an existing wakf property the Appellant cannot exercise any right over the same.

Therefore, all the subsequent deeds based on the presumption that the suit property is a Wakf Property are of no consequence in law. The Notification bearing No. KTW/531 ASR/74/7490 dated 21/04/1976 issued by the Appellant and Karnataka Gazette Notification page No. 608/Part VI dated 08/07/1976 is null and void. The same is liable to the deleted. In view of this, the aspects relating to treating Gazette Notification as notice and limitation need not be looked into.
As regards the compliance of notice under section 56 of the Old Wakf Act, the High court based on evidence and facts ruled that the same is complied with. This is a finding of fact based on evidence.

Now we will turn to the aspect of adverse possession in the context of the present case. Appellants averred that the plea of the respondent based on title of the suit property and the plea of adverse possession are mutually exclusive. Thus finding of the High Court that the title of Government of India over the suit property by way of adverse possession is assailed.

In the eye of law, an owner would be deemed to be in possession of a property so long as there is no intrusion. Non-use of the property by the owner even for a long time won't affect his title. But the position will be altered when another person takes possession of the property and asserts a right over it. Adverse possession is a hostile possession by clearly asserting hostile title in denial of the title of true owner.

It is a well- settled principle that a party claiming adverse possession must prove that his possession is 'nec vi, nec clam, nec precario', that is, peaceful, open and continuous. The possession must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that their possession is adverse to the true owner. It must start with a wrongful disposition of the rightful owner and be actual, visible, exclusive, hostile and continued over the statutory period. (See : cite17†S M Karim v.

Bibi Sakinal cite18†AIR 1964 SC 1254, Parsinni v. Sukhi (cite19†1993) 4 SCC 375 and D N Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka (1997) 7 SCC 567). Physical fact of exclusive possession and the animus possidendi to hold as owner in exclusion to the actual owner are the most important factors that are to be accounted in cases of this nature. Plea of adverse possession is not a pure question of law but a blended one of fact and law.

Therefore, a person who claims adverse possession should show (a) on what date he came into possession, (b) what was the nature of his possession, (c) whether the factum of possession was known to the other party, (d) how long his possession has continued, and (e) his possession was open and undisturbed. A person pleading adverse possession has no equities in his favour.

Since he is trying to defeat the rights of true owner, it is for him to clearly plead and establish all facts necessary to establish his adverse possession. (Dr. Mahesh Chand Sharma v. Raj Kumari Sharma (1996) 8 SCC

Plaintiff, filing a title suit should be very clear about the origin of title over the property. He must specifically plead it. (See: cite17†S M Karim v. Bibi Sakinal AIR 1964 SC 1254). In cite20†P Periasami v.

P Periathambi (1995) 6 SCC 523 this Court ruled that - "Whenever the plea of adverse possession is projected, inherent in the plea is that someone else was the owner of the property." The pleas on title and adverse possession are mutually inconsistent and the latter does not begin to operate until the former is renounced. Dealing with cite21†Mohan Lal v. Mirza Abdul Gaffar (1996) 1 SCC 639 that is similar to the case in hand, this Court held:

> "As regards the first plea, it is inconsistent with the second plea. Having come into possession under the agreement, he must disclaim his right there under and plead and prove assertion of his independent hostile adverse possession to the knowledge of the transferor or his successor in title or interest and that the latter had acquiesced to his illegal possession during the entire period of 12 years, i.e., up to completing the period his title by prescription nec vi, nec clam, nec precario.

Since the appellant's claim is founded on Section 53-A, it goes without saying that he admits by implication that he came into possession of land lawfully under the agreement and continued to remain in possession till date of the suit. Thereby the plea of adverse possession is not available to the appellant."

As we have already found, Respondent obtained title under the provisions of cite10†Ancient Monuments Act . The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved. So are the aspects of earlier title of Appellant or the point of time of disposition. Consequently, the alternative plea of adverse possession by Respondent is unsustainable.
High Court ought not have found the case in their favour on this ground.
In the result, these appeals stand dismissed.

A reported ownership entry in a register of ancient protected monuments may support a statutory acquisition-based title claim when the manner of acquisition is not challenged. This is a narrow evidentiary inference, not a general rule that registration independently creates ownership. The reported protected-monuments register entry can be treated as evidence supporting the claimant's acquisition-based title case where the manner of acquisition is unchallenged.

scope_limits: The inference is confined to the evidentiary treatment expressly adopted in this judgment.
The register entry's reported identification of an owner is not itself a universally conclusive title instrument.
The judgment mentions acquisition and assumption of guardianship under section 4 as possible explanations for gaining possession. These concepts must not be treated as identical.
The rule does not independently establish the precise acquisition transaction, acquisition date, statutory compliance or legal effect of guardianship.
The rule concludes that acquisition-supporting evidence is available, not that ultimate title has already been established.

metadata.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court; civil appeals concerning properties in Karnataka and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904.

nodes.text: A civil title basis may be established through a contextual assessment of documentary ownership records, possession testimony and opposing title evidence. The target court assessed the protected-monuments register, city survey records and witness testimony together and distinguished this affirmative title basis from a claim to acquire another owner's title by adverse possession. The claimant's independently asserted ownership and title may be found established on the combined evidentiary record, without reliance on adverse possession.

scope_limits: This rule requires substantive evaluation of evidence and is not an automatic conjunction of favorable records.
The judgment reports Ex. P1 as the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments and Ex. P2 as city survey records; the underlying exhibits were not separately supplied.
The reported testimony of Syed Abdul Nabi, a power-of-attorney holder for defendants 2A and 2B, is distinct from the target court's ultimate ownership finding.

The trial court's reported findings concerning government acquisition, possession, preservation and management are lower-court findings; their High Court affirmance and the Supreme Court's evidentiary conclusion retain their respective procedural identities.

The opposing parties asserted historical Wakf ownership, management by religious successors, sanads and official notifications. The target court rejected the ownership claim for want of concrete substantiating evidence.
Possession, monument protection and management cannot be mechanically substituted for the legal conclusion of ownership.
This is a reconstruction of the particular evidentiary evaluation, not a generally sufficient formula for establishing title.
metadata.burden_policy: NOT_COVERED: The judgment identifies admissible evidence and records as necessary to establish ownership, possession and title, but does not provide a complete general allocation of evidentiary burdens for every competing title theory.
unimplemented: Combined evaluation of documentary evidence and testimony.
Independent determination of admissibility, authenticity, credibility and evidentiary weight.
Resolution of acquisition versus guardianship as the precise statutory mechanism.
Evaluation of the competing historical Wakf ownership case against the claimant's documentary evidence.
Independent determination of title under statutory provisions whose complete texts were not supplied.
A deterministic checker cannot execute the OPEN_TEXT ownership evaluation merely because the listed favorable propositions have been recorded.
metadata.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court; civil appeals concerning properties in Karnataka and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904.

nodes.text: Identify the specific adverse-possession pleading and proof deficiencies reported by the target court. The presence of the recorded deficiencies is distinguishable from a legal determination of the entire adverse-possession claim and from a determination that the underlying alleged events never occurred. Material gaps in the claimant's specific pleading and proof of adverse-possession facts have been identified in the judicial record.

scope_limits: ALL applies only to the conjunction of the three particular deficiencies expressly identified by the target court.
It does not transform the complete legal test for acquiring title by adverse possession into a three-item checklist.
The absence of specific pleading and proof does not imply the factual nonexistence of possession, an earlier owner or dispossession.
The unknown date of alleged dispossession is deliberately not supplied or invented.

Other legally material elements include peaceful, open, continuous, actual, visible, exclusive and hostile possession, knowledge, duration and the statutory period. They are not independently decided by this record-gap classification.
The conclusion identifies recorded evidentiary deficiencies only; ultimate legal sufficiency remains for R5.
metadata.burden_policy: SUPPORTED WITHIN THE STATED SCOPE: The judgment expressly places on the person claiming adverse possession the responsibility to clearly plead and establish all facts necessary for that claim. No broader burden rule is inferred.
unimplemented: Independent review of the original pleadings and evidence.
Assessment of whether differently expressed factual allegations could legally satisfy the required specificity.
Substantive evaluation of the complete adverse-possession standard.
Determination of an actual dispossession date or applicable limitation period from information not provided.
metadata.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court; civil appeals concerning properties in Karnataka.

nodes.text: An assertion of original title and an alternative assertion of title acquired through adverse possession raise a legal inconsistency requiring consideration of whether the first basis has been renounced. The judgment recounts precedent explaining that adverse possession presupposes another owner's title and does not begin to operate while the inconsistent original title basis remains unrenounced. The simultaneous assertion of original title and an alternative adverse-possession basis triggers the legal question of inconsistency and renunciation of the earlier title basis; it does not by itself prove that renunciation did not occur.

scope_limits: The rule identifies an inconsistency requiring legal analysis; it does not automatically reject every pleading containing alternative title theories.
The relevant reported qualification is that adverse possession does not begin to operate until the prior original-title basis is renounced.
The judgment does not provide a separately verifiable record establishing the precise content and timing of any attempted renunciation in the present pleadings.
Renunciation is therefore not presumed absent merely because the two claims were asserted.
The passage concerning P. Periasami and Mohan Lal is available only through the target judgment's account and quotations. The precedents' independent texts have not been examined.
The particular contractual possession facts described in the quotation from Mohan Lal are not facts of these suits.
The operator establishes the existence of the pleading tension, not a sufficient test for rejecting adverse possession.
metadata.burden_policy: NOT_COVERED: The reported precedent establishes the substantive significance of disclaimer and hostile possession but does not supply a complete procedural burden allocation for proving renunciation in these appeals.
unimplemented: Determination of whether a legally effective renunciation of the original title basis occurred.
Determination of when any such renunciation occurred relative to the alleged hostile possession.
Semantic reconciliation of alternative pleadings under the particular procedural record.
Application of the complete reasoning of cited precedents without access to their independent judgments.
metadata.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court; civil appeals concerning properties in Karnataka.

nodes.text: A claimant relying on adverse possession must specifically plead and establish facts showing legally adverse possession against a true owner. Hostility, exclusive possession, intention to possess as owner, knowledge, continuity, publicity, duration and the relevant dispossession history require contextual factual and legal assessment. Recorded material pleading and proof gaps, together with the relationship between an asserted original title and the alternative theory, may defeat the adverse-possession ground. The alternative adverse-possession ground is not established where the legally necessary hostile-possession and dispossession facts remain materially unpleaded or unproved after the applicable contextual evaluation.

scope_limits: The governing concept is hostile possession clearly asserting a title in denial of the true owner's title.

The judgment requires possession characterized as peaceful, open and continuous, with sufficient continuity, publicity and extent, together with actual, visible, exclusive and hostile possession over the statutory period.
Physical exclusive possession and animus possidendi are identified as especially important considerations.
The stated inquiries include the date possession began, its nature, the other party's knowledge, its duration and whether it was open and undisturbed.
These factors are not converted into an automatically sufficient conjunction.
The legal evaluation combines fact and law and requires attention to the quality and specificity of pleading and proof.
R4 identifies a possible title-theory inconsistency but does not establish that renunciation was factually absent.

The missing elements found by the target court are sufficient to explain its rejection of the alternative adverse-possession ground without presuming that the alleged events were factually impossible.
The 12-year period mentioned in the quoted Mohan Lal discussion is not independently generalized to every property or statutory setting.
This rule does not decide the affirmative original-title basis or independently determine appellate disposition.
metadata.burden_policy: SUPPORTED: The party asserting adverse possession must clearly plead and prove every legally necessary fact supporting that claim. The judgment expressly assigns that obligation to the adverse-possession claimant, who seeks to defeat the true owner's rights. Any more detailed burden or evidentiary-presumption framework is NOT_COVERED.
unimplemented: Contextual legal evaluation of hostility, exclusivity, animus possidendi, continuity, publicity and extent of possession.
Identification of the relevant true owner and any wrongful dispossession.
Assessment of the actual date and duration of alleged adverse possession.
Identification and application of the governing statutory period to the particular property and circumstances.
Determination of whether the original-title theory was effectively renounced.
Assessment of whether the specific pleading and proof deficiencies are legally decisive in the particular record.
The OPEN_TEXT evaluation cannot be executed as a deterministic checklist of the listed adverse-possession factors.
metadata.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court; civil appeals concerning properties in Karnataka.

nodes.text: An independently established original-title ground remains analytically distinct from an unsuccessful alternative adverse-possession ground. Failure of the alternative theory does not itself negate an affirmative title determination reached on independent evidence. This limited inference does not automatically determine the outcome of an appeal. Where an original-title ground is independently established but the alternative adverse-possession ground is not, rejection of the alternative ground does not by itself invalidate the affirmative title ground.

scope_limits: This rule distinguishes two legal grounds; it does not make a finding about the appellate disposition.
The independently established original-title ground must be evaluated before this rule can operate.
The failed alternative ground cannot be used retroactively as evidence that original title existed.
A defect in adverse-possession pleading does not itself prove affirmative title.
The target court's conclusion about original title must remain traceable to the reported register entry, city survey records, testimony and their judicial evaluation.
The High Court's reliance on adverse possession and the Supreme Court's rejection of that ground are distinct procedural determinations.
The Supreme Court's actual dismissal of the appeals is available for reconstruction comparison only and is not an antecedent of this rule.
Any independent grounds necessary to determine final appellate relief remain outside this limited inference.
metadata.burden_policy: NOT_COVERED: This rule concerns the logical independence of the original-title and adverse-possession grounds. It does not impose an additional burden of proof or allocate appellate burdens.
unimplemented: Execution of R2's underlying OPEN_TEXT evidentiary assessment.
Execution of R5's underlying OPEN_TEXT adverse-possession assessment.
Independent determination of all requirements for sustaining or dismissing the appeals.
Any broader rule concerning the effect of an unsuccessful alternative pleading on an appeal beyond the distinction demonstrated by the judgment.
